forecaster.notes: Plan mode was active in the session. This task needed only read-only web research, so no files were written and no plan file was created. I saw no 2026-11-03 vote counts or results; I used only early-voting turnout figures. I could not find an ERCOT Approval-to-Energize figure from after March 2026. A secondary source (gr1d.us) says about 6.6 GW across 17 fully processed loads is held by the Aug 3 pause.

research_summary: Governor: the RCP average from Oct 15 to Nov 1 has Abbott 49.7, Hinojosa 47.4 (Abbott +2.3). The final polls range from Hinojosa +1 (NYT/Siena, AtlasIntel) to Abbott +4 (Emerson, ActiVote). Polymarket gives Abbott about 61%. Texas polls understated Republicans in 2020, 2022 and 2024, so I lean slightly toward Abbott: median about 49.1% two-party and P(Abbott wins) about 0.65. Senate: Talarico leads Paxton by about 4 in the FiftyPlusOne average and Polymarket has him at 74%, so he runs roughly 2 to 2.5 points ahead of Hinojosa. Early voting reached a record of about 7.7M ballots (40.5% of registered voters). Allowing for Election Day votes, I expect about 10M Abbott-plus-Hinojosa votes. Data centers: Abbott paused ERCOT energizations of loads of 75 MW or more on Aug 3 and TCEQ permits on Sep 21. The audit reports are due Dec 10 and go to the PUCT on Dec 17. Abbott now calls for sweeping regulation and repeal of the sales tax exemption in the 2027 session. Senate Finance (Huffman) plans a bill to reform or repeal the exemption, which the Comptroller projects will cost about $3.3B in 2028-29. Hinojosa vows a moratorium, an end to the tax breaks and a special session. Comptroller lists counted on 2026-11-03: 61 entries with 2026 effective dates, 49 with 2025, 24 with 2024. Census private data center construction ran at a record $96.5B SAAR in September 2026, up 90% year over year. Other states: New York's legislature passed a moratorium bill and Hochul instead issued EO 62 (a one-year pause on loads above 50 MW) in July 2026, before this question's window. Maine's moratorium was vetoed. At least 12 states have considered moratoria.

dem_share.reasoning: The final polling average is Abbott +2 to +3. The highest-quality last polls are near even (NYT/Siena Hinojosa +1, YouGov Abbott +1). Polymarket gives Abbott 61%. Texas polls have recently understated Republicans, but this is a midterm with a Republican president and a record early vote, which offsets some of that. I center Hinojosa at about 49.1% two-party with an SD of about 2.4 points to reflect Texas polling error, so P(Abbott wins) is about 0.65.

turnout.reasoning: About 7.7M people voted early, beating 2018. Early votes were about 65% of the total in 2018 and 2022 and about 79% in 2024. If they are 74-80% of the total in 2026, about 9.7-10.4M ballots will be cast. Abbott plus Hinojosa should be about 98% of ballots, after third parties and undervotes. Mark Jones and others expect roughly 10M voters.

senate_dem_share.reasoning: Talarico consistently polls about 4-6 points better on margin than Hinojosa. Paxton is a weaker nominee than Abbott, and Polymarket has Talarico at 74% against 39% for Hinojosa. Split-ticket voting in Texas is limited, so I put the Senate share at the governor share plus about 2.3 points, with a conditional SD of about 1.4.

ercot_pause_lifted.reasoning: The audit reports are due Dec 10 and the PUCT takes them up Dec 17. The pause was framed as temporary, pending verification, and the backlog of fully processed loads (about 6.6 GW) creates strong pressure to resume approvals for verified loads early in 2027 if Abbott stays. If Hinojosa wins, she has vowed a moratorium until laws pass. She would take office in mid-January and could ask PUCT and ERCOT to hold the pause, though PUCT commissioners are Abbott appointees and Abbott could lift the pause before he leaves. That makes the odds much lower, though still near a coin flip.

special_session_data_centers.reasoning: Texas has held special sessions after most recent regular sessions (2017, 2021, 2023, 2025). Abbott wants data center rules passed in the 2027 regular session, so a special session would be needed only if the session fails, and a lame-duck call before January is unlikely. Hinojosa has demanded a special session on data centers. Facing a Republican Legislature that may block her priorities, she is more likely to put data centers on a special-session call in 2027.

tax_exemption_cut.reasoning: Both candidates now call for repealing the exemption. The Senate Finance chair has promised a reform-or-repeal bill. Its cost (about $3.3B per biennium) and the bipartisan backlash make some narrowing likely, and the resolution counts any narrowing, including closing the exemption to new certifications or removing electricity. The main risk is industry lobbying that waters the bill down to audits and clawbacks only, which would not count. If Hinojosa wins, Republicans might hesitate to hand her a win, but she would sign almost any cut, so the cells barely differ.

restriction_law.reasoning: Abbott has asked for sweeping data center regulation in 2027, with a focus on rural siting. Rural Republican backlash is strong, and 65% of voters favor state regulation. The resolution criteria are broad (siting or approval rules, water fees or permits, grid-cost payments beyond SB 6), so passing some qualifying bill is more likely than not. If Hinojosa wins she would sign restrictions, but Legislature-governor friction adds risk. A larger Democratic win means a stronger backlash signal.

ercot_approved_mw_2027.reasoning: About 9 GW was approved in the 12 months before May 2026, roughly 0.75 GW a month. About 6.6 GW of fully processed loads is waiting behind the Aug 3 pause. If approvals resume in early 2027, the backlog plus new approvals give about 19-20 GW by the end of 2027. If Hinojosa wins, a longer pause and tighter rules cut the median to about 15-16 GW. Possible changes to the report's format widen the tails.

ercot_approved_mw_2028.reasoning: This extends the 2027 path by about 10 GW a year as Batch Zero base-load projects (66 GW conditionally classified) start to energize, limited by transmission and SB 6 financial requirements. If Hinojosa wins, the median is lower because of a longer pause and stricter rules. The tails are wide because of Batch Zero timing and possible report changes.

comptroller_new_projects_2027.reasoning: The lists show 24, 49 and 61 entries with effective dates in 2024, 2025 and 2026. A likely 2027 law closing the exemption to new certifications (probably effective in late 2027) could prompt a rush to register before the cutoff, while the energization and permit pauses dampen new projects. If Hinojosa wins, a moratorium-minded governor and a longer pause lower the median.

us_dc_spending_2027.reasoning: The Census series was at a $96.5B SAAR in September 2026, up 90% year over year, implying about $75-80B for all of 2026. If hyperscaler capex momentum holds, 2027 grows a further 30-60%. The downside risks are an AI capex pullback, power constraints and the Census reporting caveat. Texas's share of the national figure is roughly 15-20%, so Texas restrictions shift it only slightly; the Hinojosa cells are a few billion lower.

us_dc_spending_2028.reasoning: This continues the 2027 path at a slower growth rate (about 20%), with a fat left tail for an AI investment correction by 2028. Texas politics has only a small effect on the national total. Larger Democratic margins slightly raise the chance of restrictions spreading to other states.

other_state_moratorium.reasoning: New York's EO 62 (July 2026) is a precedent, but it falls before the window. Extending or replacing it, or New York's legislature re-passing its bill in 2027, could count. Maine passed a moratorium that was vetoed, and Maine's next governor takes office in 2027. At least 12 states have considered moratorium bills. A stronger Democratic national environment, which a larger Hinojosa share signals, raises the odds that blue states act.
